senses: One who practices astrology; an astrologer.
examples: So the king sent his painters to Moses and they brought back a picture of him. The king called his phrenologists and astrologists and asked them, "What kind of man is this?"
According to Accurso, there is evidence that advice from astrologists had no effect on Hitler's actions.

senses: A tempo mark directing that a passage is to be played in a grand and noble style
A passage having this mark
ety: Borrowed from Italian grandioso, from Latin grandis (“great, grand”) (English grand). Doublet of grandiose.

senses: An extension to feminism that incorporates respect for women of all races and classes.
ety: From woman + -ism. Coined by Alice Walker in 1983.
examples: Although womanism raises the issue of gender, it simultaneously offers a distance from the “enemy,” in this case, Whites generally and White women in particular.
In line with femalism, African womanism is committed to the quest for total freedom of the colonized African men and women.

senses: That which tranquillizes or soothes.
One of a demographic class of young, socially-conscious, urban professionals.
ety: From urban + -ite (“resident of a particular area”).

senses: Construction using whatever materials were available at the time.
Something constructed with whatever materials were available at the time.
A rhetorical style that brings together excerpts or samples of others' rhetoric in some constructive way (to produce, for example, synthesis, extension, or beauty).
An instance of this rhetorical style's use, or a work produced with its use.
A biting midge (family Ceratopogonidae).
Stale brioche, spread with almond cream and sliced almonds and then baked
ety: From French bostock, of uncertain origin; Russian восто́к (vostók, “east”) has been suggested.
examples: To make a single portion of bostock, cut a slice of brioche ½ to ¾ inch thick.
It was also where I had my first taste of bostock, a French pastry originally devised as a thrifty way to use up stale brioche.
It’s walk-up only, so plan on enjoying your tarts, bostocks, sourdough loaves, and coffee (drip only; no espresso drinks) elsewhere.

senses: To stitch (sew with a needle).
To shut or close.
To use a technique for knitting garments such as sweaters in the round without interruption for openings or sleeves until the end.
ety: From Scots steek, from Middle English steke (“to enclose”) and Middle Dutch steken (“to stitch”). Noun from Scots steek (“stitch”), from Middle Dutch steek (“stitch”). More at stick, stitch.

senses: New or novel, usually in reference to Latin American culture.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish nuevo. Doublet of new.
examples: What young adults have managed to come up with is either nuevo hipster or ultra-nerd, but almost always a bland imitation of the past.
In Chicago, a favourite resto is Topolobampo, celebrity chef Rick Bayless's shrine to nuevo Mexican cuisine.

senses: A piece or music serving as an overture, interlude or ritornello.
A small symphony orchestra.
ety: Borrowed from Italian sinfonia. Doublet of symphonia, symphony, tsampouna, and zampogna.

senses: A popular condiment in many countries, usually mayonnaise-based.
Not irradiated.
Perforated, as in the manner of a sieve.
Any of a class of nickel/iron alloys that have a high magnetic permeability.
A grain crop, a hybrid of wheat and rye, that gives a high yield.
Any particular variety of triticale.
ety: Blend of Latin trīticum (“wheat”) + Latin sēcale (“rye”).

senses: An athlete who competes in the hurdling event.
A person who is neither a citizen nor colonial/imperial subject of the state whose military they join.
A member of a legion, such as the American Legion, or of any organization containing the term legion in its title (e.g. the French Foreign Legion).
ety: From legion + -ary. From Latin legiōnārius. Doublet of legionnaire.

senses: A Roman racing chariot drawn by four horses abreast.
A team of four horses, or sometimes other animals, especially as used in chariot racing.
ety: From Latin quadrīgae, literally "four yoked", from quattuor (“four”) + iugum (“yoke”).

senses: A synthetic replacement for vasopressin.
ety: Desmo: word-forming element used in scientific compounds and meaning "band, bond, ligament," from Greek desmos "bond, fastening, chain," related to dein "to bind," from PIE root *dē- "to bind." Pressin: from vasopressin, the hormone that desmopressin is an analogue of, that causes increased blood pressure.

senses: An explosive manufactured from a variety of materials, including nitroglycerine, wood meal and nitrates.
An explosive composed of nitrobenzene, saltpetre, sulfur, and kieselguhr.
A naturally occurring carbonaceous material formed from coal, natural coke.
examples: He was pleased with bellite, he found that carbonite made more fumes than bellite, but the explosive he liked best was ammonite.

senses: The reagent of known concentration and volume used in titrations.
A form of soccer played indoors, with five players per team.
ety: Borrowed from Portuguese futsal, a blend of futebol de salão (literally “hall football”).

senses: Strongly disapproved of.
Belittled; insulted.
ety: From Latin dēprecātus, past participle of dēprecor (“to pray against (a present or impending evil), pray for, intercede for (that which is in danger), rarely imprecate”), from de (“off”) + precor (“to pray”).

senses: Leather made from the hide of a cow or similar animal.
A whip made of that material.
examples: Mr. Plummer was a miserable drunkard, a profane swearer, and a savage monster. He always went armed with a cowskin and a heavy cudgel.

senses: Capable of being generalized.
One who attempts to draw attention to themselves by their behavior.
One who exposes their genitalia (or female nipples) in public.
Synonym of exhibitioner (“student who is awarded an exhibition”).
Having the nature of an improvisation.
ety: By surface analysis, improvisation + -al, or, by surface analysis, improvise + -ation + -al.

senses: One who partakes in clubbing: one who frequents nightclubs.
One who clubs: one who hits (something or someone) with a club.
examples: I'd rather go with my clubber friend Brandon than to have Catherine sleep in my room.

senses: The state or condition of being cardiotoxic.
A lover of books.
A presacral vertebra.
To discourage or demotivate by means of a disincentive.
A company which, or a person who, grants franchises.
A person who uses a snorkel to do snorkeling.
Held in suspension.
Holding in suspension.
To resume the consumption of alcohol, drugs, etc.; to reverse a period of detox.
ety: Humorous opposite to detox; see re-.

senses: A chocolate shop.
ety: From French chocolaterie. By surface analysis, chocolate + -erie.
examples: The sheer nerve of the woman—opening a chocolaterie just in time for Lent.
It is telling, though, that there remains a fine line between the chocolaterie and the church. Vianne never enters the church, and the priest never tastes the chocolates in the chocolaterie.
I worshipped her body with mine and tasted every single part of her with the wild satisfaction of a gourmand in a chocolaterie.

senses: The notional area of land able to be farmed in a year by a team of 8 oxen pulling a carruca plow, usually reckoned at 120 acres.
ety: From Medieval Latin carūcāta (“ploughland”), from Latin carūca (“chariot; coach; carruca”). Compare French charrue (“plough”).

senses: An officer whose business it is to ascertain the contents of casks.
ety: From Middle English gauger, gager, equivalent to gauge + -er. Compare Old French gaugeur, jaugëor.
